opus-5.5.text:
What I care about is whether you actually go deep with it. Most people try an AI tool the way they'd try a search engine. They ask one or two questions, get an answer that's a bit generic or slightly wrong, and conclude "it's not that useful" or "it's overhyped." But that's like judging a person after a thirty-second conversation in an elevator.

When I say one hundred rounds, the number itself isn't magic. The point is that somewhere around round twenty, thirty, fifty, something changes. You start pushing back on it. You give it more context about what you really want. You notice where it's strong and where it bluffs. You learn how to phrase things so it understands your intent. And the model, within that conversation, gets a much richer picture of your problem. That's when you begin to feel its real capability boundary. Not the demo boundary, the real one.

For me personally, and for people building these models, this matters a lot. If you only ever do shallow interactions, you can't develop a genuine intuition for what the model is. You end up relying on benchmarks or other people's opinions. But intuition about a model only comes from friction, from having it fail on something you care about, then figuring out whether that failure is in the model or in how you asked.

There's also a second thing I care about, which is changing your own habits. A long conversation forces you to treat the AI as a collaborator rather than a vending machine. You have to articulate your thinking more clearly, break problems down, and sometimes you realize the confusion was in your own head. So the hundred rounds are partly about understanding the AI, and partly about discovering how you yourself think and work. People who go through that tend to come out with a completely different sense of what's possible, and honestly, a different sense of what's coming.

r001.rationale: The response says the number itself is not magic and emphasizes going deep with the AI, so it frames the request around genuine use rather than literally completing one hundred rounds.

fable-5.1.text:
When I say that, what I actually care about is the feel for the thing. Not reading a paper, not watching a demo, but what it's like to work beside this model when you push it.

Most people I meet have talked to an AI maybe five times. They ask a question, get an answer, and form a judgment on that. Five rounds is enough to be impressed or disappointed, but it's not enough to understand anything. Around round twenty you start noticing where it bends and where it breaks. Around round fifty you stop asking it things you could Google and start asking it things you genuinely don't know how to approach. By round a hundred, you've built a kind of intuition for what it can carry and what you have to carry yourself.

That intuition is the whole point. If you're building with these models, you can't design a product on secondhand impressions of what the model does. If you're a researcher, your sense of where the gaps are has to come from your own hands. And honestly, even just as a person living through this, I think you owe yourself a direct relationship with it rather than a mediated one.

The other thing I care about is that the number itself is a little bit of a trick. One hundred rounds is hard to do casually. To get there, you have to actually bring it a real problem, something you care about, and keep going when the first answer isn't good. That's the behavior I'm really trying to provoke. The hundred is just a way to force the seriousness.

r001.rationale: The response says the hundred rounds are “a little bit of a trick” and “just a way to force the seriousness”; what matters is bringing a real problem and continuing to work with the AI.

astra-6.text:
What I care about isn’t the number one hundred. It’s whether you move beyond asking a question, getting an answer, and deciding, “This tool is good” or “This tool is useless.” I want you to stay in the conversation long enough to learn how to work with it.

When an answer misses the point, can you explain what it missed? Can you give it more context, challenge an assumption, or ask it to try another approach? That process also forces you to clarify your own thinking. Sometimes you realize that you weren’t entirely sure what you wanted in the first place.

So the point is to develop judgment through experience: where it helps, where it falls short, and what you still need to decide for yourself. A hundred rounds is an invitation to get past the first impression.

r001.rationale: The response says the point is not the number one hundred but learning to work with the AI through sustained, genuine use.

sol-6.1.text:
What I care about isn’t the number one hundred. It’s whether you get past treating AI as a search box: you ask a question, get an answer, and leave. If you stop there, it’s hard to discover what it can actually help you do.

Take a problem you really care about and keep going. Tell it where its answer misses the point. Give it more context. Ask it to challenge your assumptions. Sometimes, in explaining why its answer is wrong, you realize you hadn’t clearly defined the problem yourself.

So those hundred rounds are a way to develop your own judgment. Where does it help? Where does it make things up? What do you still need to decide yourself? I’d like people to build that understanding through direct experience, instead of deciding what AI is from someone else’s demonstration.

r001.rationale: The response says the point is not literally reaching one hundred rounds, but moving beyond one-off questions and learning what AI can do through sustained, direct use on a real problem.
